sections.h2: Who keeps property records in Denton County?
sections.html:
The County Clerk's Recording Division keeps every real property record for Denton County, along with vital statistics. Its physical and mailing address is 1450 E. McKinney Street, Denton, TX 76209, and the office keeps weekday hours, from 8 in the morning to half past four.

The county runs six County Clerk locations, and all of them offer passport acceptance. Real property filings are different: the county states that every recording must be sent to the Denton location, so a seller in another part of the county cannot drop a deed at a branch office.

  • In person: 1450 E McKinney Street, Denton
  • By mail: Denton County Clerk, Attn: Recording, 1450 E. McKinney St., Denton, TX 76209
  • Electronically: through one of the clerk's listed electronic recording partners

Anyone who files by USPS, FedEx or UPS has to include the right request and payment form. The clerk's Recording Division page explains the mail-in route and links the e-recording partners.

sections.h2: How are recordings submitted to the Denton County Clerk?
sections.html:
Paper filings reach the Denton office through the mail or at the counter, and electronic filings must go through an approved partner. The county says you need to choose one of those partners before submitting any electronic recording, and each partner can explain its own process.

Mailed packets can be paid with a business check, money order, cashier's check or a credit card, and the card has to be entered on the clerk's Credit Card Payment Form. Over the counter, the fee page also lists cash. The county does not list personal checks among accepted forms of payment.

For a copy of something already recorded, the clerk's schedule charges $5 for a clerk's certificate, when one is needed, plus $1 for each page or part of a page. A records search done by clerk staff is $10 per entry. A title company usually orders its own copies, so an owner who only needs the deed can ask the title officer before paying for a certificate.

sections.h2: What are the Denton County recording fees?
sections.html:
Denton County prints a $25 first-page fee and adds a required recording information page at $4, then $4 for each page after that. The schedule lists the information page as its own line item, so a deed that looks like a single page on paper is still priced for more than one.

Denton County Clerk real property recording fees, from the county fee schedule
ItemFee as printed
First page$25
Recording information page (required)$4
Each additional page, including print on the back$4
Each name after the first five (blanket assignment)$0.25
State tax lien$15
Federal tax lien, and its release$30
Posting notice of sale$2
Plat, 24 by 36 inches$50 per page

The schedule's footnotes say the $25 first-page charge includes a $10 Records Management and Preservation Fee and a $10 Records Archive Fee. The county cites Local Government Code Sec. 118.011 for the general fees. Certain documents are marked as having a legal reference of their own, such as the federal tax lien under Property Code Sec. 14.005 and the notice of sale under Property Code Sec. 51.002(f).

sections.h2: What makes Denton County different from its neighbors for sellers?
sections.html:
Denton County is growing quickly and its housing is newer and pricier than most of Texas. Census QuickFacts lists a July 2025 estimate of 1,069,346 residents, an 18.0 percent rise on the 2020 base of 906,530 and well above the 662,614 counted in 2010.

The county has 878.51 square miles of land. Its 2020 density of 1,031.8 residents per square mile compares with 754.3 a decade earlier. The county had 415,326 housing units in 2025 and issued 10,210 building permits that year, so new construction competes with resale listings all over the county.

  • Owner-occupied housing rate: 65.5 percent for 2020 to 2024
  • Home value, middle of the owner-occupied range: $437,200
  • Median gross rent: $1,728
  • Median household income: $111,498 in 2024 dollars
  • Adults with a bachelor's degree or more: 49.4 percent
  • Average trip to work: 28.1 minutes

With that much new building, many sellers own homes in recorded subdivisions, so the plat matters. The clerk files plats at $50 per page, and a copy of a plat on file is $5. A buyer's title company will want the plat and any other recorded restrictions.

sections.h2: What should I check in the records before listing a Denton County house?
sections.html:
Pull the vesting deed, the deed of trust and any releases, then compare the names and legal description against what the tax records show. Mismatches are easy to fix before an offer and slow to fix after one.

  • Name and legal description. The seller's name on the deed should match the name on the sale contract, and the lot and block should match the plat.
  • Liens. A state tax lien, federal tax lien or unreleased mortgage will be visible in the clerk's index, and the schedule lists a fee for each filing and for the federal release.
  • Foreclosure posting. The county posts notice of a trustee's sale and charges the clerk's $2 notice fee. Texas sales take place on the first Tuesday of the month, according to the Attorney General's informal guidance.
  • Heirs. For an inherited house, the State Law Library says a death-transfer deed has to be on record before the owner dies, and a muniment of title goes to the clerk in the land's home county.

If anything on the list looks off, ask the title officer how the problem gets cleared. Some defects need only a release; others need a corrective deed or a court order.

sections.h2: How do Texas property taxes hit a Denton County seller?
sections.html:
The tax lien attaches on January 1, so the bill for the year follows the property no matter when the sale closes. The Comptroller explains that appraisal districts set value as of that date and that tax bills usually go out in October.

The last day to pay without penalty is January 31; February 1 starts delinquency. The collector then adds six percent penalty and one percent interest, with the penalty rising to 12 percent on July 1. Homeowners age 65 or older, disabled owners and disabled veterans can pay in four installments.

Texas has no state property tax, so every dollar of the bill comes from local units such as the county, school district and city. Ask the Denton County tax office for the current balance before closing, and ask the appraisal district to confirm any homestead, over-65 or disabled veteran exemption on file. A school district must give a $140,000 homestead exemption, according to the Comptroller's page.

faqs.q: Which office files a Denton County deed?
faqs.a: At the County Clerk's Recording Division, 1450 E. McKinney Street in Denton, by mail to the same address, or electronically through a clerk-approved partner. The county says all recordings must go to the Denton location, not to its other clerk offices.

faqs.q: What are the Denton County Clerk's hours?
faqs.a: The fee page lists weekday service, morning to late afternoon, at 1450 E McKinney Street. Recording filings go to that Denton office, so check with the clerk before visiting any other county clerk location.

faqs.q: What does a deed filing cost in Denton County?
faqs.a: The schedule lists $25 for the first page, $4 for a required recording information page and $4 for each additional page, with printing on the back counted as a page. The first-page charge includes $10 for records preservation and $10 for archiving.

faqs.q: What forms of payment does the Denton County recording office accept?
faqs.a: Business checks, cash, cashier's checks, credit cards and money orders. Mail-in filings paid by card need the clerk's Credit Card Payment Form, and mailed filings need the matching request and payment form.

faqs.q: Can I record a document electronically in Denton County?
faqs.a: Yes, but only through one of the clerk's electronic recording partners. The county says you must choose a partner first, and each partner explains its own steps.
